title: Is a Website AI Chatbot Worth It? Mostly No for Shops
h1: A chat widget, or just a phone number?
meta: Website AI chat carries the Air Canada risk — you own what it says (Moffatt v. Air Canada, 2024). For most small shops a phone number and fast callback beats it.
short: Website chat widgets carry real legal risk and rarely beat a phone number with a fast callback. For most small shops it's a no.
statLabel: Moffatt v. Air Canada (2024): the business was held liable for what its website chatbot told a customer

body.answer: For most small shops a website AI chatbot adds legal risk and a layer of friction without beating a phone number and a fast callback.
body.html:
Every website vendor wants to sell you a chat widget. Little bubble in the corner, "Hi! How can I help?" It feels modern. The question is whether it actually gets you more jobs than the phone number you already have — and whether it quietly creates problems the vendor won't mention.

For most small contractors, the answer is no. A homeowner with a problem wants to talk to a person who can show up. A chat bubble is a detour. And an AI-powered one is a detour with legal risk baked in.

body.h2: The Air Canada problem lives in your chat widget
body.answer: Anything your website bot tells a customer is something your business is on the hook for.
body.html:
Start with the risk, because it's the part nobody sells you on. In Moffatt v. Air Canada (2024), a tribunal held the company liable for false information its website chatbot gave a customer — the business owned what its bot said. That was a website chat widget, exactly like the one you're being sold.

So when your widget tells a customer "we can do that for about $200" or "we're available Saturday," that's your promise now. The bot improvises to be helpful, and you're left honoring whatever it made up. That's a lot of downside for a corner bubble.

body.h2: What a chatbot competes against: a fast callback
body.answer: A phone number plus a quick human callback beats a chat widget on the only thing that matters — speed to a real answer.
body.html:
Set the risk aside and the chatbot still has to earn its spot. What's it competing against? A phone number and a human who calls back fast. And fast wins: responding in 5 minutes instead of 30 makes you up to 100x more likely to connect with a lead, and 21x more likely to qualify it (Lead Response Management study, Prof. James Oldroyd).

A chat widget doesn't beat that. At best it captures a name you then have to follow up on anyway. At worst it holds a fake conversation, quotes something wrong, and sends the lead off thinking they've been handled. Pair your phone number with missed-call text-back and you've got the speed without the robot. More on that in speed to lead for contractors.

body.answer: Only consider one if it's a dumb lead-capture form that never quotes or promises anything.
body.html:
If you insist on a widget, make it a dumb one: a form that grabs a name and number and nothing else. No AI holding court with your customers, no prices, no promises. The less it says, the less it can cost you.

For most shops, though, the right move is to skip it and spend the attention on answering faster. We put the AI versions through the wringer in is an AI receptionist worth it. If you want a human reviewing your lead flow instead of a bubble, talk to a person.

faq.q: Should a small contractor put an AI chatbot on their website?
faq.a: For most small shops, no. It carries real legal risk — in Moffatt v. Air Canada (2024) the business was held liable for what its chatbot told a customer — and it rarely beats a phone number with a fast human callback.

faq.q: Is a website chat widget better than a phone number?
faq.a: Usually not. A homeowner with a problem wants a person who can show up, and speed wins: 5-minute vs 30-minute response makes you up to 100x more likely to connect (Lead Response Management study). A widget is a detour at best.

faq.q: What's the safest way to use website chat?
faq.a: Make it a dumb lead-capture form that grabs a name and number and nothing else. No AI quoting prices or making promises. The less the widget says, the less it can put you on the hook for.
